Then, for every cycl,e it calculates SoC bthe Coulombmb counting technique</div><div>SoC(for that time step)=1-(cummulative Ah used/Max capacity)</div><div>NOTES:</div><div>a. It skips rows that have &gt;100 seconds between them (data logging lapses)</div><div>b. each row=time step, thousands of such time steps together=cycle&nbsp;</div><div><br></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="500" width="341.5" x="6.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-13" connectable="0" parent="A7MCSDpipdGKFvhA_Wse-10" style="group" value="" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="2398" width="364" x="6.5" y="1143" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-14" parent="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-13" style="whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="364" width="364" y="73" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-1" edge="1" parent="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-13" source="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-15" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"> <mxPoint x="486.59682144657245" y="86.70967741935465" as="targetPoint" /> </mxGeometry> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-59" edge="1" parent="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-13" source="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-15" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"> <mxPoint x="240.10006713867188" y="630" as="targetPoint" /> </mxGeometry> </mxCell> <mxCell id="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-15" parent="5mvFuiNa0TlY9W_V5Uf1-13" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<div><b><font style="font-size: 24px;">topmodule.v</font></b></div><div>1.clk-system clock at 100MHz, divided to a smaller 25MHz</div><div>2. BUFG: global clock buffer, if we used normal clock signal pathlot of skew across the huge circuit, lifts the signal out of the logic and puts in it in clock tree (signal splits into symmetrical branches&nbsp; making the skew same everywhere, heavy duty electrical amplifiers present at branch intersections to boost the electrical signals)</div><div>3. slow_clk (25MHz) passed through this BUFG and used by SPI, coloumb counter, LSTM&nbsp;</div><div>4. sclk: external serial clock which leaves FPGA goes to ADC (slow_clk) divided even further (500kHz)</div><div><br></div>" vertex="1"> style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));"><font style="font-size: 24px;">.py</font></b></div><div>1. ML models and FPGAs are very sensitive to ordering and distribution of data (for example, FPGAs use fixed-point arithmetic, hence you can't have outliers)</div><div>2. Real-world battery datasets are at a fully charged or discharged state for hours while being in the mid ranges (40-60% for a very small time), so if these numbers appear most of the time, the ML model will have a bias towards that&nbsp;</div><div>Solution: creates 2 buckets of current &gt;0.5A and current &lt;0.5A</div><div>3. discards 80% of idle data in the 2nd bucket and sorts the remaining data according to the SR no (LSTM requires time series data)</div><div>4. Divides SoC into 20 buckets, each 5,% and checks the F ratio between all buckets &lt;20&nbsp;</div><div>5. To maintain precision in Q.8.8 math on FPGAs, we need the current in 0-5,A , so if there are spikes of current (glitches) like&nbsp; 2.5A,A it will scale to the normal operating region to a really small value; hence,wee need to discard those, discard everything outside (-5, 5) range</div><div>6.&nbsp;</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="500" width="341.5" y="14" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<div><b style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));"><font style="font-size: 24px;">train_model_qat.py</font></b></div><div>1. Hardware-aware training done, normal models are designed for 32-point floating math, less accurate, piecewise linear approximations of sigmoid and tanh functions&nbsp;<br></div><div>2. data chopped into 50 time step sequences&nbsp;</div><div>Reason: LSTM doesn't look at single data points, it needs to look at a trend to see if a battery is charging or draining, looks at 50 seconds of v, t, and soc to make a prediction&nbsp;</div><div>3. Any voltage below 1V is flagged as a glitch&nbsp;</div><div>4. After every training epoch, check the size of the weight to see if it exceeds&nbsp;</div><div>2.0</div><div>5. Validation split is 0.2&nbsp;</div><div>6. The&nbsp; Adam optimizer is used, which adapts the learning rate for each weight&nbsp;</div><div>7.EarlyStopping is&nbsp; used, which stops training if accuracy on validation data stops improving after 25 epochs</div><div>8. ReduceLRonPlateaus reduces learning rate by a factor of 0.5 if it's stuck on a loss plateau for 10 epochs</div><div>9. MinMaxScaler adjusts inputs between 0 and 1</div><div>10. MaxNorm for LSTM is 2, for dense is 3</div><div><br></div><div><br></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="500" width="341.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="gyMlgycVIwHT3zTDMpnz-32" q16.16&nbsp;</div><div>2. first grabs the exact neural network layer using .get_layer() then calls get_weights() to grab the exact weights in numpy array format</div><div>3. Keras stores LSTM weights in a 2D matrix&nbsp; but BRAM needs a flat list&nbsp; so&nbsp;W[inp*64 + gate_offset + neuron] used to calculate exact location in bram</div><div>4. 64 because 16 neurons x 4 gates, inp is 0 for voltage, etc&nbsp;</div><div>5. rgb(255, 255, 255));"><span style="font-size: 24px;"><b>minmax_preprocess.v</b></span></span></div><div>1. The parameters generated are used here to scale inputs</div><div>2. x(input in q8.8, with 32 sign bits padded so 40.8) * scale (q16.16) gives q56.24 output, but a 48-bit accumulator stores q24.24, chopping off the top 32 redundant sign bits, then this product is shifted by 16 bits to make it q24.8, and the offset is shifted by 8 bits to make q16.8. When added,&nbsp; it takes the 8 fractional bits anthe d bottom 8 integer bits&nbsp;</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="500" width="341.5" x="6.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-115" connectable="0" parent="gyMlgycVIwHT3zTDMpnz-4" style="group" value="" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="3541" width="370.5" x="634" y="535" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-116" parent="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-115" style="whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="364" width="364" y="73" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-121" edge="1" parent="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-115" source="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-118" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"> <Array as="points"> <mxPoint x="177.33" y="651.67" /> <mxPoint x="756.33" y="651.67" /> <mxPoint x="756.33" y="552.67" /> <mxPoint x="1196.67" y="552.67" /> </Array> <mxPoint x="1196.678059895834" y="177.86836751302098" as="targetPoint" /> </mxGeometry> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-118" parent="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-115" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<div><span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));"><span style="font-size: 24px;"><b>bnorm_preprocess.v</b></span></span></div><div>1. Same procedure</div><div>2. minmax strictly processes the values between 0 and 1, batch normalization is required to keep the value centered around 0, which prevents the lstms activation layer from getting saturate,d and optimizes numbers for a fixed-point MAC array</div><div><br></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="500" width="341.5" x="6.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-120" parent="gyMlgycVIwHT3zTDMpnz-4" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="mm_valid" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="30" width="60" x="1067" y="603" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="vAGTRB8VlI7csKN2kacn-146" parent="gyMlgycVIwHT3zTDMpnz-4" style="whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="<div style="text-align: left;"><font face="Helvetica"><br></font></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><font face="Helvetica">1.&nbsp;<span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">computes the core linear algebra of an LSTM gate: </span><code style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">(W * x) + (U * h) + b</code></font></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><font face="Helvetica">2.Insteadd of computing one neuron at a time, 16 parallel 48-bit accumulators, using DSP blocks</font></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><font face="Helvetica">3. does not instantiate all 320 multiplications at once, would require 320 DSP slices, uses 16 DSP slices over 22 cycles (20 input+hidden, 1 activation, 1 bias)</font></div><div style="text-align: left; Dividing dt/2600 to convert seconds to hours takes LUTs and DSPs</div><div>2. Time sampling is done every 10 seconds, to convert this to q16.16 10/3600 needs to be multiplied by 2^16 (65536)</div><div>3. area under current curve=(I prev+I current) * dt/2, current is in q8.8 format</div><div>4. to multiply a q8.8 number by q16.16, output is q24.24 but the accumulator is meant to store q16.16 hence 8 bit right shift is done then 1 more bit right shift needed as divide by 2 style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">1. 4 inputs, 16 hidden state output&nbsp; from the previous time step) glued together, these 20 (weight x input) in 16 neurons=320 multiplications x 4 gates=1280 multiplications</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">2. The hidden state output also goes to the dense layer</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">3. Every neuron has 4 gates: forget gate, input gate, cell state candidate, output gate (every doing 20 weights x 20 numbers)</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">4. After each gate is done with its multiplication and accumulation, it adds a bias at the end (16 neurons x 4 gates=64 biases)</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">5. All these 1280+64 (1344) numbers are stored in BRAM</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><br></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><br></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">The LSTM Layer FSM works in this manner&nbsp;</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">IDLE ---start_calc----&gt;FORGET_GATE-----mac_done---&gt; INPUT GATE -----mac_done----&gt;CELL_CANDIDATE---mac_done---&gt; UPDATE_CELL---&gt;UPDATE_H---&gt;DONE----&gt;IDLE</div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;"><br></div><div style="text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;">6. div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 340px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1429px; margin-left: 9px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.div: 1. takes 10 battery files from the NASA dataset
2 .cleans the data (foexample,eg if current is NaN or voltage temperature is empty, fillswith they last known value)
3. calculates the maximum capacity of a battery
how: calculates time difference between each row and Ah used up by each row, Ah used up calculated by step_ah =current*time
4.Itt does this for all cycles, and the cycle with the highest totalAHh is the max capacity
5. Then, for every cycl,e it calculates SoC bthe Coulombmb counting technique
SoC(for that time step)=1-(cummulative Ah used/Max capacity)
NOTES:
a. It skips rows that have >100 seconds between them (data logging lapses)
b. each row=time step, thousands of such time steps together=cycle

div.div: 1.clk-system clock at 100MHz, divided to a smaller 25MHz

2. BUFG: global clock buffer, if we used normal clock signal pathlot of skew across the huge circuit, lifts the signal out of the logic and puts in it in clock tree (signal splits into symmetrical branches making the skew same everywhere, heavy duty electrical amplifiers present at branch intersections to boost the electrical signals)
3. slow_clk (25MHz) passed through this BUFG and used by SPI, coloumb counter, LSTM
4. sclk: external serial clock which leaves FPGA goes to ADC (slow_clk) divided even further (500kHz)

div.div: 1. ML models and FPGAs are very sensitive to ordering and distribution of data (for example, FPGAs use fixed-point arithmetic, hence you can't have outliers)

2. Real-world battery datasets are at a fully charged or discharged state for hours while being in the mid ranges (40-60% for a very small time), so if these numbers appear most of the time, the ML model will have a bias towards that
Solution: creates 2 buckets of current >0.5A and current <0.5A
3. discards 80% of idle data in the 2nd bucket and sorts the remaining data according to the SR no (LSTM requires time series data)
4. Divides SoC into 20 buckets, each 5,% and checks the F ratio between all buckets <20

5. To maintain precision in Q.8.8 math on FPGAs, we need the current in 0-5,A , so if there are spikes of current (glitches) like 2.5A,A it will scale to the normal operating region to a really small value; hence,wee need to discard those, discard everything outside (-5, 5) range

div.div: 1. Hardware-aware training done, normal models are designed for 32-point floating math, less accurate, piecewise linear approximations of sigmoid and tanh functions
2. data chopped into 50 time step sequences
Reason: LSTM doesn't look at single data points, it needs to look at a trend to see if a battery is charging or draining, looks at 50 seconds of v, t, and soc to make a prediction
3. Any voltage below 1V is flagged as a glitch
4. After every training epoch, check the size of the weight to see if it exceeds
5. Validation split is 0.2
6. The Adam optimizer is used, which adapts the learning rate for each weight
7.EarlyStopping is used, which stops training if accuracy on validation data stops improving after 25 epochs
8. ReduceLRonPlateaus reduces learning rate by a factor of 0.5 if it's stuck on a loss plateau for 10 epochs
9. MinMaxScaler adjusts inputs between 0 and 1
10. MaxNorm for LSTM is 2, for dense is 3

div.div: 1. converts weights and biases from floating point arithmetic to q16.16
2. first grabs the exact neural network layer using .get_layer() then calls get_weights() to grab the exact weights in numpy array format
3. Keras stores LSTM weights in a 2D matrix but BRAM needs a flat list so W[inp*64 + gate_offset + neuron] used to calculate exact location in bram
4. 64 because 16 neurons x 4 gates, inp is 0 for voltage, etc
5. Using minmax scaler values decided during training, it converts those values to q16.16
6. Similarly, bnorm values taken and weights values converted to q16.16

div.div: 1. The parameters generated are used here to scale inputs

2. x(input in q8.8, with 32 sign bits padded so 40.8) * scale (q16.16) gives q56.24 output, but a 48-bit accumulator stores q24.24, chopping off the top 32 redundant sign bits, then this product is shifted by 16 bits to make it q24.8, and the offset is shifted by 8 bits to make q16.8. When added, it takes the 8 fractional bits anthe d bottom 8 integer bits

div.div: 1. Dividing dt/2600 to convert seconds to hours takes LUTs and DSPs
2. Time sampling is done every 10 seconds, to convert this to q16.16 10/3600 needs to be multiplied by 2^16 (65536)
3. area under current curve=(I prev+I current) * dt/2, current is in q8.8 format

4. to multiply a q8.8 number by q16.16, output is q24.24 but the accumulator is meant to store q16.16 hence 8 bit right shift is done then 1 more bit right shift needed as divide by 2 is involved so total 9 bit shift then the middle part of the accumulator [23:8] extracted as ah_out

div.div: 1. 4 inputs, 16 hidden state output from the previous time step) glued together, these 20 (weight x input) in 16 neurons=320 multiplications x 4 gates=1280 multiplications

div.style: text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;

div.div: 2. The hidden state output also goes to the dense layer

div.style: text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;

div.div: 3. Every neuron has 4 gates: forget gate, input gate, cell state candidate, output gate (every doing 20 weights x 20 numbers)

div.style: text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;

div.div: 4. After each gate is done with its multiplication and accumulation, it adds a bias at the end (16 neurons x 4 gates=64 biases)

div.style: text-align: left; forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important;

div.div: 5. All these 1280+64 (1344) numbers are stored in BRAM
